articles.title: Tinie Tempah to visit Scunthorpe after online campaign
articles.summary: His 2010 hit Pass Out included the lyrics "I been Southampton but I've never been to Scunthorpe".
articles.body:
The rapper Tinie Tempah has confirmed he will visit Scunthorpe, after an online campaign was started by a local fan to get him to the town.

His 2010 number one hit Pass Out included the lyrics "I been Southampton but I've never been to Scunthorpe".

In a video on social media, he said: "I can't wait to come down to Scunny, and meet the wonderful people. It's been long overdue, see you soon guys."

Ben Johns, who started the campaign, added: "To see everybody get involved with it from Scunthorpe United to John Leggott College, loads of different people around the town, as well as people on the internet who aren't even from Scunthorpe but want to see it happen. It's just been amazing to see."

In the social media video, the rapper thanked Johns for all of his "hard work" towards the campaign, which involved securing 5,000 pre-saves for his new album in return for a visit to the town.

He said he was "so thankful and grateful to all the people of Scunthorpe" and he "can't wait to party" with them.

Tempah spoke to BBC Newsnight in August about the pressures grassroots music venues face and his new album, which was inspired by UK nightlife.

He said he thought "this is the time" to visit the town.

Johns, who is from Scunthorpe, told BBC Radio Humberside : "I think it's really going to be a special night when Tinie Tempah turns out and he performs in the town and he gets people excited."

In a statement, Tempah's management said: "We are looking forward to planning something special for the incredible fans based in Scunthorpe."

articles.title: 6,500-year-old Indigenous sacred site in Arizona partially destroyed by Trump administration’s border wall construction; 50-foot corridor cuts through 272-foot geoglyph that predates Egypt’s first pyramid by 2,000 years
articles.summary: New research has revealed that the Las Playas Intaglio, a sacred Indigenous geoglyph in Arizona, is at least 6,500 years old, making it the oldest
articles.body: New research has revealed that the Las Playas Intaglio, a sacred Indigenous geoglyph in Arizona, is at least 6,500 years old, making it the oldest scientifically dated geoglyph in the Americas. The discovery comes months after the fish-shaped earthwork was partially damaged by federal contractors working on the Trump administration’s second border wall through the Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge. Previously believed to be around 1,000 years old, the site has now been linked to an ancient period of Indigenous history predating Egypt’s first pyramid, Peru’s Nazca Lines and the initial construction of Stonehenge.The findings, published in the September issue of The SAA Archaeological Record, were reported by researchers David S. Whitley and Ronald I. Dorn. Their study identifies the Las Playas Intaglio as the oldest scientifically dated geoglyph in the Americas.The researchers used a technique known as varnish microlamination dating, which examines microscopic layers of rock varnish and compares them with regional records of ancient climatic conditions. They analysed stones collected from the intaglio in 1979, with three samples supporting a conservative age estimate of between 6,500 and 7,300 years.Since the rock varnish formed after the earthwork was created, the researchers noted that the geoglyph could be even older.Its estimated age places the creation of the site roughly 2,000 years before Egypt’s first pyramid, 4,000 years before Peru’s Nazca Lines and 1,500 years before the first construction of Stonehenge.Ancient site partially damaged during border wall constructionThe discovery has drawn renewed attention to the damage caused to the site on April 23, when contractors working for US Customs and Border Protection drove heavy equipment through the intaglio while preparing land for a second border barrier.According to the Center for Biological Diversity, the construction work created a roughly 50-foot-wide scraped corridor that cut through part of the 272-foot-long figure and the surrounding wildlife refuge.Russ McSpadden, Southwest conservation advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the newly established age of the site made its destruction even more significant.“This discovery makes an already devastating loss even more profound. It’s a cultural and historical atrocity,” McSpadden said. He added that the destruction had harmed the deep history of Indigenous communities and called for accountability over the damage.“People deserve to know what warnings were given and why safeguards, if they existed, failed,” he said, urging Congress to seek records and testimony about who authorised and carried out the work.Geoglyph holds deep cultural and religious significanceLas Playas lies within the ancestral homeland of the Tohono O’odham, Hia-Ced O’odham and other Indigenous tribes. Intaglios are large figures created by removing dark stones from desert surfaces to expose the lighter ground beneath.According to the researchers, such sites are important to Indigenous cultural and religious traditions, tribal identity and continuing relationships with ancestral lands. The newly established age of the Las Playas Intaglio offers further insight into the long history of Indigenous communities in the region.McSpadden compared the destruction to the hypothetical bulldozing of part of Stonehenge to make way for a wall, arguing that Indigenous heritage deserves the same level of protection as other internationally recognised cultural sites.Border construction raises concerns over other sacred sitesThe damage to the Las Playas Intaglio follows other instances of destruction and threats to culturally significant places in the region. In February 2020, blasting at Monument Hill, a burial ground sacred to the O’odham in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, drew concern over the impact of border wall construction.Construction has also affected saguaros, which the Tohono O’odham Legislative Council recognised as O’odham persons and kin in a May 2021 resolution condemning their destruction.In January 2025, the San Xavier District Council called for the protection of the sacred jaguar and its habitat and movement corridors from border barriers and other threats. Construction of primary and secondary walls has also been reported in the San Rafael Valley, an important jaguar corridor between Mexico and the United States.Meanwhile, plans for a second parallel wall have raised concerns about Quitobaquito Springs, a sacred O’odham oasis within Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. Conservation advocates warn that bulldozing and groundwater pumping could permanently damage the water system that sustains rare aquatic wildlife.Calls for greater protection of Indigenous cultural heritageThe destruction has renewed questions about how ancient and sacred sites are protected during major infrastructure projects. UNESCO’s 2003 Declaration concerning the Intentional Destruction of Cultural Heritage recognises that such destruction harms humanity as a whole and calls for preventive measures and sanctions consistent with international law.The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples also affirms Indigenous peoples’ rights to protect their cultural heritage, traditions and religious practices.Meanwhile, US Customs and Border Protection had been accepting public comments on 225 miles of secondary border wall construction across Arizona through October 12, according to the information provided by the agency. The deadline has now passed as of October 13, 2026.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Northwestern Ontario to ditch seasonal time change
articles.summary: But the rest of the province will keep changing their clocks, as provincial law prevents province-wide change until New York State and Quebec also make the s...
articles.body:
See more Toronto Sun on Google — save as a Preferred Source

Portions of Northwestern Ontario are transitioning to permanent daylight saving time.

That news came from Queen's Park early Tuesday afternoon, a move provincial officials say will align portions of the province that set its clocks to the central time zone with Manitoba, which last month opted to permanently keep their clocks on summer time.

"Through the collective efforts of communities and First Nations across the northwest, we've led a process to build consensus the right way, with detailed and nuanced considerations," said Ontario's Indigenous Affairs Minister Greg Rickford in a statement.

"What has emerged is unanimous support across the region to move to permanent daylight saving time, and our government is proud to support the people of northwestern Ontario as we make this decision, together."

Last month, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew announced his province would permanently adopt daylight saving time as of Nov. 1.

Rest of Ontario will remain on two-time system

The changes announced Tuesday would see Ontario communities west of the 90th meridian follow suit, and will not turn their clocks back on Nov. 1.

Communities in Ontario's eastern time zone will, however, continue to change their clocks twice a year.

"Providing certainty and predictability is essential to supporting strong communities and a competitive economy," said Attorney General Doug Downey in the same statement.

"By keeping this part of the province aligned with Manitoba, our government is taking a practical, common-sense approach to avoid unnecessary disruptions and ensure economic stability in communities that reside in Ontario's central time zone."

In Nov. 2020, Ontario passed Bill 214, the Time Amendment Act, which mandates Ontario permanently adopt daylight saving time — but only under certain conditions.

Ontario cannot, as a whole, permanently lock its clocks until the province of Quebec and New York State follow suit.

Under U.S. federal law, individual states can opt out of daylight saving time and remain on standard time all year, but cannot adopt daylight saving time permanently without a specific act of Congress.

This means Ontario will remain on a two-time system unless federal legislation is passed in the United States allowing New York State to make the change.

articles.title: Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says
articles.summary: Yemen has reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of the total coming in last four weeks.
articles.body:
Suspected cholera cases in Yemen have tripled in the past three weeks, the World Health Organization (WHO) warns, as civilians continue to escape renewed fighting and seek safety in unsanitary camps.

Ramped up combat, which has pushed more than 200,000 people to flee their homes, the WHO said in a report on Tuesday, driving suspected cases from 217 in the week of September 6-12 to 647 in the week of September 27 to October 3.

“Families fleeing conflict are now facing another threat from diseases that can be prevented and treated,” said Annette Heinzelmann, the UN agency’s emergency director for the region.

“Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities.”

This year, the global health watchdog said, Yemen had reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths, with a quarter of the suspected cases occurring in the last four weeks.

Five governorates hosting large numbers of displaced people in the southwest – Abyan, Lahij, al-Dhalea, Taiz and Aden – account for 92 percent of reported cases, they reported. The disease has also reached remote displacement camps in Hadramout in the country’s east that are particularly difficult for medical teams to access.

Cholera has ebbed and flowed for years as the conflict in Yemen has continued. In 2024, the WHO warned that the country was facing the “highest burden” of a global cholera outbreak. In 2017, a wave of the disease infected hundreds of thousands and killed at least 2,000.

Yemen was already suffering one of the “world’s worst humanitarian crises ” and has seen an escalation of food insecurity and disease since fighting reignited between the Houthis and the government in July, shattering four years of fragile calm.

Cholera is an acute intestinal infection that spreads through food and water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, often from faeces. It causes severe diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.

Contracting the illness can be deadly when not treated with oral rehydration or antibiotics for more severe cases.

The Geneva-based WHO said it had only secured $3.78m of the $31m needed for its 90-day emergency response in Yemen.

The funding is intended to help expand disease surveillance in displacement sites, deploy rapid response teams, strengthen cholera treatment and improve infection prevention in health facilities and cholera treatment sites.

articles.title: Maserati driver gets suspended sentence after killing woman in Pontypool crash
articles.summary: Ronald Dowling overtook a vehicle in heavy rain before aquaplaning, skidding and hitting another car.
articles.body:
A Maserati driver who killed a woman and seriously injured two others has been given a suspended prison sentence.

Ronald Dowling, 66, overtook a vehicle in heavy rain before aquaplaning, skidding across the carriageway and hitting Sharon Berry's car in the fatal crash at New Inn, Pontypool, on 26 October 2023.

His wife, Kim Dowling, was left paralysed, and passenger Jane Beedell also suffered extensive injuries.

Dowling, who previously pleaded guilty to causing death and serious injury by careless driving, was sentenced to 27 months in prison, suspended for two years.

On Tuesday, at Merthyr Crown Court, Judge Celia Hughes told him: "Your consequences should live with you for life."

The court heard Dowling, from Caerphilly, was driving with his wife and their lifelong friend, who they were taking to a hospital appointment, when the collision happened.

Despite wet and windy conditions, heavy rain and high levels of surface water, he was travelling at 76mph (122 km/h) just three seconds before the crash.

After aquaplaning, the defendant crashed into a stationary black Audi A3 driven by Sharon, who had pulled over because of the weather conditions.

She suffered catastrophic injuries and spent three months in hospital before her death in January 2024.

In a victim impact statement, her son Luke Berry, who is expecting a child, described the family's loss as immeasurable, saying his mother would never get the chance to meet her grandchild.

He said: "She was loving, caring and would do anything to make sure I was OK.

"My family will never be the same without her."

The court was also told Jane Beedell suffered multiple injuries in the crash, including chest and elbow injuries, bruising, wounds to her fingers, bleeding on the brain and multiple fractures to her ribs.

She was placed in an induced coma for weeks, and told the court the crash had left her struggling with "fear, anxiety and depression".

"I used to be confident, strong and an outgoing individual," she said, explaining how she now relies on family and friends for daily support and struggles with everyday tasks, finding it difficult to go out alone.

After 48 years working in the civil service, Jane said she had lost her job and now relied on benefits.

She said she was devastated by the changes to her life, adding: "I sometimes feel guilty I survived".

The court heard how Kim Dowling was left paralysed with a broken back and neck and unable to speak after her voice box was removed following the crash.

Mitigating, Dowling's barrister said the defendant felt "deep regret and remorse for the loss of life", along with "strong feelings of guilt and emotional distress".

The court heard that every time Dowling looked at his wife, he was reminded of what he had done.

The case was initially brought as dangerous driving, but the charges were later changed to careless driving, to which he pleaded guilty.

Dowling had previously been disqualified from driving for six months about 15 years ago after reaching 12 penalty points, the court heard.

However, he had no previous convictions despite years of long-distance driving for work and was described as a man of "good character" who was a full-time carer for his wife.

During the sentencing, Judge Hughes said Sharon Berry had suffered a "senseless death", adding that "no amount of sentence given to Dowling would bring her back".

Dowling was sentenced to 27 months in prison for causing death by careless driving and two counts of causing serious injury by careless driving, suspended for two years.

He was also disqualified from driving for four years, ordered to complete 250 hours of unpaid community work and pay £1,630 in prosecution costs.

articles.title: Britain faces ‘new era’ of security threats from Iran and Russia, MI5 says
articles.summary: Britain’s MI5 boss Ken McCallum warned of a range of threats posed by Russia, Iran, China, AI and terrorist groups.
articles.body: LONDON — Iran is escalating its campaign of threats on British soil, expanding attacks beyond dissidents abroad and Jewish sites to now focusing on harder military targets, the country’s domestic intelligence chief said Tuesday. MI5 Director General Ken McCallum was speaking less than two weeks after the United States rushed to withdraw its bombers from a key air base in England, with American officials saying there had been reports of a possible Iranian drone attack. Giving a wide-ranging “annual threat update” at MI5’s Thames House headquarters in London, McCallum warned that Britain and Europe had “entered a new era of national security,” which he likened to the shift that came after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. His speech comes at a moment of tumult not just for the Middle East and Ukraine, which continue to be ravaged by war, but also the rest of Europe, which has suffered so-called hybrid aggression from Moscow and Tehran including sabotage, arson and cyberattacks. European governments are now openly telling people to stockpile food and prepare for more of their taxes to be spent on defense, warning that Russia may launch a direct attack on their soil. MI5 is now devoting more resources than it had during the Cold War to countering threats from countries such as Russia, Iran, China and others, McCallum said. “Russia remains aggressor No. 1, as Putin’s Kremlin continues to lash out at the U.K. and its allies,” he added. But another arch belligerent is Iran, whose leaders have been “attempting to expand their hybrid campaign” of “using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations and Israeli sites,” the spy chief said. “Much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities, with whom I want to express solidarity,” he said. But this year has seen a shift of “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.” Over the past year, intelligence operations have led to more than 50 Iran-linked arrests in Britain, he said. McCallum made reference to the incident last month at RAF Fairford, the military base in rural England from where the U.S. had been launching bombers involved in the assault against Iran. He declined to give details, citing ongoing investigations and operations, but said the case was “not unique.” Details are hazy, but in the early hours of Sept. 27, a member of the public called the police after spotting three vans in a country lane near the base. Seven men in their 20s, one of them a dual British-Iranian national, have been arrested and released on bail. Authorities said they found only gasoline in the vehicles. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers in Parliament on Monday that the incident “is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed” by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the powerful political, military and economic group that holds huge sway in the country. A week after the incident, Washington hastily withdrew its bombers from the base because, according to two U.S. officials, of reports of a possible drone attack against the site. On Tuesday, McCallum downplayed fears that Iran could mount such a complex attack, saying it has so far been hiring unsophisticated criminals for operations in the United Kingdom. But he warned that could change. On Russia, McCallum said its military and intelligence services “are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare,” being careful not to trigger NATO’s Article 5 threshold, in which other countries would be expected to defend their allies. “We see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding,” he said. “The whole aim of hybrid tactics is to try to intimidate us.” Within the U.K.’s “multifaceted relationship with China” — Beijing is a major trading partner to London — MI5 has been focused on efforts by the Chinese government “to conduct espionage, coercion or democratic interference.” On Al Qaeda and the Islamic State terrorist group, or ISIS, MI5 still has to respond “to attempts to carry out mass casualty attacks,” he said. But perhaps the gravest warning came when it came to artificial intelligence, which he said in the future could be used by terrorist groups and other actors to create new “bioweapons.” And “beyond misuse of AI by human adversaries sit the potential risks posed by AI itself,” he said. “Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are. Is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel. And deserves the serious attention it is getting, including in MI5.”

articles.title: ‘EC should regain credibility’: Ashok Lavasa says poll panel must regain public trust amid SIR controversy
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa on Tuesday said the Election Commission of India (ECI) was facing an unprecedented level of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa on Tuesday said the Election Commission of India (ECI) was facing an unprecedented level of controversy and urged the poll body to regain public trust amid protests over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Drawing a parallel with cricket, Lavasa said the credibility of an election depended on people believing that the poll panel was impartial.“If people feel that the umpire is not neutral, they will question the winning team's victory as well,” he said while addressing a citizens' convention in Kolkata virtually, according to news agency PTI.Lavasa's remarks came as opposition parties intensified their protests against alleged “vote chori”, demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise.Opposition leaders have taken to the streets in recent days and clashed with police in New Delhi.“The EC should regain its credibility and people's trust. The Election Commission of India, whose position is very high and possibly the highest among all public institutions, is today mired in controversies and people are taking to the streets to protest,” Lavasa said.Questions over dissent within Election CommissionThe former election commissioner referred to an Indian Express report that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected on record at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.The objections reportedly came even as the nationwide SIR exercise was being overseen by the full commission.Lavasa questioned the lack of publicly available meeting minutes, saying it was difficult to establish whether decisions had been taken unanimously or by a majority.“This casts a doubt in the minds of the people whether the decisions of the Election Commission, including on the SIR, were unanimous or taken by majority,” he said.He also said the Election Commission had not provided an authentic clarification on the reported differences between its members.“Some press statements have been issued, but those create more questions and generate more doubts than they answer,” Lavasa said.The poll panel has maintained that differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberations in any institution. It has also said that all its orders carry full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures.The EC added that all three commissioners, as well as its officers, were authorised to offer suggestions to improve the electoral system.Lavasa flags concerns over SIRLavasa said the SIR exercise had triggered widespread anxiety over voting rights, adding that people had not been as concerned about protecting their right to vote in the preceding 16 months.“The EC's decision to conduct the SIR took everyone by surprise,” he said.He noted that the Election Commission had conducted special revisions of electoral rolls in the past under the Representation of the People Act and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, but argued that the current exercise had created an unprecedented level of public concern.Lavasa also questioned the approach of categorising electors into three age groups based on their dates of birth under the Citizenship Act.The Constitution, he said, requires the Election Commission to enrol all those who meet the eligibility criteria under Article 326, which provides for voting rights for Indian citizens aged 18 and above who are not of unsound mind or disqualified under any law.“But unfortunately, with the tactics deployed this time, the goal is not to include. Possibly the priority is to exclude people from the voter list on the suspicion that they are not Indian citizens and not on evidence,” he said.Referring to West Bengal, Lavasa said nearly 60 lakh people's voting rights had gone under adjudication during the SIR, apart from those excluded from the draft electoral rolls. He said the EC had not adequately considered the proximity of the Assembly elections and the difficulty of adjudicating such a large number of cases in time.Lavasa added that around 33 lakh names had been restored to the voter list after adjudication.Prakash Raj joins criticism of SIRActor-activist Prakash Raj, who also addressed the convention, described the SIR as the “most dangerous disease” and alleged that it was undermining democracy.“Even before Gyanesh Kumar came (as the CEC), they broke parties in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and Bihar,” he said, accusing the BJP leadership of seeking to divide people through the SIR into those who could vote and those who could not.Raj also alleged that the West Bengal Assembly elections were conducted in an “illegal” manner following the revision exercise, claiming that voter names had been selectively deleted. He said opposition parties had come to believe they were contesting “fixed” elections.The convention was organised by CPI(M) leader Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya and retired bureaucrat Jawhar Sircar.The protests over the SIR have also prompted a wider political confrontation between the opposition and the ruling BJP.Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has vowed to continue the INDIA bloc's campaign against alleged electoral irregularities, while Union home minister Amit Shah has accused the Congress of trying to shield infiltrators by opposing the exercise.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2005, WWE’s Kane built a 6,924-square-foot home on 78 wooded Tennessee acres, including a 2,400-square-foot gym; he later listed the private retreat for $800,000
articles.summary: Explore the luxurious 6,924-square-foot estate of WWE's Kane located in Jefferson City, Tennessee, featuring expansive wooded acreage, a private gym, and more, now on the market for $800,000.
articles.body: WWE wrestler Glenn Jacobs, also known as Kane, had a 6,924-square-foot home that was custom-built for his family on 78 acres in Jefferson City, Tennessee, in 2005. The property included private woods, a swimming pool, a koi pond and trails for biking, four-wheeling and horseback riding, while a detached 2,400-square-foot garage doubled as a gym.Jacobs put the estate on the market in 2015 for $800,000, and told Realtor.com that he did not really want to leave the property, but the family's insurance business in Knoxville had made the roughly hour-long commute rather difficult. The house sat on a hill at the end of a quarter-mile driveway that climbed about 250 feet to the top, and the listing described a three-bedroom contemporary home surrounded by woods.The gym was built separately from the houseJacobs had a detached 2,400-square-foot garage that was built as a full gym, and gave him a dedicated space for training away from the house. Jacobs said he worked out five or six times a week at the time of the listing, and made the gym equipment also a part of the sale, although its inclusion was negotiable. He had previously been known for heavy strength training and told Realtor.com that he could once bench press 525 pounds.The main house had a finished basement with a game room that included a poker table, foosball table, pool table and wet bar. The master suite included a bathroom with dual vanities, custom wood cabinetry and a large garden tub in a windowed tower that overlooked the surrounding hills. Jacobs described the property as private, and the estate's wooded acreage kept the house away from the road. The property also included trails and recreational areas in addition to the house and gym.The property was designed for privacy and distanceThe house was positioned at the end of a quarter-mile driveway, and the road rose roughly 250 feet before reaching the home, which meant that the main residence was set well back from the public road rather than sitting directly beside it. The 78 acres that surrounded it also created a substantial buffer between the house and neighboring properties, because of wooded sections that covered much of the land.The land included wooded areas and established trails, which gave the family space to move around the estate without having to leave the property. The setting also placed the house on elevated ground, and views across the surrounding Tennessee landscape from parts of the residence were visible. The property was built around the idea of having considerable land between the home and everything outside it rather than being a large house placed on a small celebrity-style lot.That arrangement also helped explain why the property could feel secluded despite being within driving distance of Knoxville, since the combination of the long driveway, elevation and wooded acreage meant that the residence was largely shielded from passing traffic and the surrounding road network. The land was therefore more than an extra feature of the sale for a family that used the property as a full-time residence, and was a central part of the estate’s design and its appeal.Kane's life had already moved beyond wrestlingJacobs had spent more than two decades working as a professional wrestler by the time the house was listed, and WWE's biography of Jacobs notes that he became known internationally as Kane and later moved into politics in Tennessee. He was elected mayor of Knox County in 2018 after his wrestling career started coming to an end.It was a period when Jacobs was still balancing his wrestling career with his family and business interests, and his decision to sell was tied to that business life instead of a reported change in the property's condition. The 2015 listing put the estate's asking price at $800,000, with Jacobs saying that he would miss the gym and the property itself, but the commute had become difficult enough that the family decided to relocate.You use AI every day. articles.body: Cornell University has suspended parties and other social events at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year as outrage mounts over its handling of a woman's allegations that she was gang-raped at a fraternity house in 2024.University president Michael Kotlikoff announced the measures on Tuesday, including a new “zero tolerance” policy under which fraternity chapters would face immediate emergency suspension for violations. The restrictions on social events at Interfraternity Council houses will remain in place until the end of the 2026-27 academic year.The university will also work with New York State Police to allow independent, trauma-informed criminal investigators to investigate sexual assault allegations on campus, a role currently handled by Cornell University Police. It will also appoint a case manager to help students reporting sexual misconduct navigate the university's procedures.“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.The announcement comes amid protests by students over the university's response to the alleged assault and fresh scrutiny of how the criminal investigation was handled.What happened at the fraternity house?The woman, identified as Jane Doe in court documents, alleges that members of the Chi Phi fraternity plied her with alcohol and drugs before several men sexually assaulted her at a party in October 2024. She filed a lawsuit last month against seven fraternity members, Cornell and others. Lawyers for two of the men have denied that their clients participated in a sexual assault, while some men questioned during the university's disciplinary proceedings said the sexual activity was consensual or that they were not involved.Jane Doe reported the incident to Cornell police in November 2024, but no criminal charges followed. Her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said she was “misled” about the status of the investigation, believing it was continuing when the inquiry had effectively ended. District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said he had concluded, after reviewing a summary of her account, that no crime had been committed. He has since reopened the investigation.New York Governor Kathy Hochul subsequently appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor, removing the case from Van Houten.Students have staged protests and a dining hall sit-in, demanding changes to the university's handling of sexual misconduct complaints. articles.title: Why advanced U.S. weapons aren’t stopping Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology. But in recent days it has appeared helpless in the face of barrages of missiles and drones fired by the Houthi rebel group from neighboring Yemen. The attacks have struck Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors and work from home. The Iran-backed Houthis, once seen as little more than a ragtag militia, have grown into a formidable fighting force. They have inflicted damage on the region’s top oil producer, threatened critical supply routes in the Red Sea and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands. The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defenses failed to stop the Houthis’ attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next. Here’s what we know and don’t know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict: Vast arsenal Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12% of all U.S. arms exports from 2021-2025. Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defense systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers. Saudi Arabia’s annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles. Huge area to defend The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia’s large size. Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country’s sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles through rugged desert areas. “Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday. At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help. Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support. President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision. Battle-tested Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn’t require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting. The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defenses. The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023. While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year. Andreas Krieg, a professor at King’s College London, said this experience in challenging Israel’s cutting-edge air defenses has given the Houthis confidence and expertise as they now strike Saudi Arabia. “They’ve learned how to over-saturate the radars,” he said. The Houthis, working with allied militias in Iraq, have also targeted Saudi oil installations, including a vital pipeline used to export oil through the Red Sea while movement through the Strait of Hormuz is limited. The Houthis have also seized territory in Yemen near the Bab el-Mandeb, a key Red Sea waterway, putting additional pressure on Saudi oil exports. Miscalculation Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, says the kingdom assumed the Houthis wouldn’t strike civilian targets like airports. Doing so marked “a paradigm shift,” he said. Ratney, now an adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Saudis now find themselves in a position where they have to respond while also trying to prevent the fighting from spinning out of control. “They can’t not strike back — they were attacked in a very brutal way by their archenemies,” he said. “They need to exert military pressure on the Houthis and then find a way to kind of deescalate.” Rather than sending troops into Yemen, the Saudis will likely launch airstrikes against the Houthis and ramp up support of nationalist forces, several analysts said. “It will be surrogate warfare,” Krieg said. A formidable force While the Houthis don’t have the firepower of Saudi Arabia, they have grown into a fearsome force controlling roughly one-third of Yemen thanks to help from Iran. The United Nations estimates that the Houthis by 2024 had recruited up to 350,000 fighters. That’s up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in the internationally recognized Yemeni government’s civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade. Ratney says the Houthis now have a “symbiotic relationship” with Iran and should not be seen as an Iranian puppet. The strikes on Saudi airports and economic assets symbolize a sharing of lessons in asymmetric warfare between the Houthis and the Iranians: how to not just puncture expensive air defenses, but also damage vulnerable energy installations and threaten global maritime routes. “Over the course of the past few years, the Iranians have been innovating and sharing that with the Houthis and it’s gone both ways. The Houthis have been innovating, and sharing it with the Iranians,” Ratney said. “It’s no coincidence that they’ve ended up with a similar approach.” Their recent military successes have made the Houthis feel “untouchable,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a fellow at Chatham House focused on Yemen. “It’s very hard to convince a man he’s going on the wrong side if he just moved forward and he has a gun in his hand,” he said. But the Houthis are now likely to suffer a brutal Saudi counterattack, he said.

articles.title: Cornell cancels fraternity parties over sexual assault case
articles.summary: The school has faced an uproar over how it handled assault allegations brought by a woman known as Jane Doe.
articles.body:
Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as the school faces backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago.

Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house.

In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the rest of the school year.

"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said.

"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.

Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.

In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".

"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.

Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.

The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.

Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault.

The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.

These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said.

Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.

Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.

State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.

Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".

He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

articles.title: Reparations activists celebrate 'important victory' after Newsom signs first-ever corporate slavery bill
articles.summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom signed AB 2599, forcing large corporations in California to disclose historical ties to slavery in a first-in-the-nation law.
articles.body: California advocacy groups are celebrating a "big, important victory" in their push for state-level reparations after Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a first-in-the-nation bill requiring large corporations to investigate and disclose historical ties to chattel slavery. Kristin Nimmers, policy and campaign manager for the California Black Power Network (CBPN) and the Alliance for Reparations, Reconciliation, and Truth, told Fox News Digital Newsom’s signature on Assembly Bill 2599 — the Truth in Disclosure Act — marks a significant milestone for corporate accountability. "There are connections right now from slavery to current wealth of individuals and current wealth of corporations whose foundation and who built the start of their companies off of slavery and off of benefits gained from slavery," Nimmers said. CALIFORNIA LAWMAKERS WANT CORPORATIONS TO DISCLOSE TIES TO SLAVERY DESPITE UNCERTAIN FUTURE FOR REPARATIONS Newsom signed AB 2599 into law Sept. 30, a move Nimmers called a "historic moment" that forces qualifying businesses operating in California to scour historical records and publicly disclose slavery-era transactions. California was the first state in the nation to establish a formal task force to study the legacy of slavery and recommend potential restitution measures. "The California Reparations Task Force spent years documenting the state's role in perpetuating racial harm and outlining this path toward repair," Nimmers said. "AB 2599 is really starting the work of identifying who really benefited from this racial harm and from slavery." Authored by Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, D-Ladera Heights, the law applies to businesses with more than $100 million in annual worldwide gross receipts that existed — or had a predecessor entity in operation — on or before Dec. 31, 1964. Once funded by the state legislature, covered companies will be required to submit sworn affidavits under penalty of perjury to the California Civil Rights Department. These disclosures must detail any historical involvement in the purchase or sale of enslaved people, the use of enslaved human beings as loan collateral, slave-related insurance policies and other financial transactions. Covered entities have until Jan. 15, 2029, to submit their initial filings. CASH PAYMENTS ARE NOT 'RULED OUT' AS CALIFORNIA COUNTY OFFICIALS PUSH REPARATIONS FOR BLACK LOCALS The progressive governor's signing of AB 2599 comes despite his cautious stance on broader, high-cost reparations initiatives. Most recently, Newsom vetoed Assembly Bill 2186, which would have exempted future state reparations payments from California's personal income tax. The bill's author, Assemblymember Tina McKinnor, D-Inglewood, told Fox News Digital Friday that the veto was disappointing. Newsom has also consistently resisted direct cash payments, which state task force recommendations estimated could cost millions per eligible recipient. He previously turned down a broader slate of cash-focused reparations measures backed by the California Legislative Black Caucus. However, Newsom did approve state funding for California universities to research and establish verification methods for descendants of enslaved Americans to determine potential eligibility for future noncash benefits. REPARATIONS ACTIVIST DOES NOT EXPECT COMPENSATION FROM NEW YORK OFFICIALS AS ACTION IS DELAYED FOR YEARS Despite those legislative setbacks, Nimmers remains optimistic about the future of reparations in the Golden State, noting that CBPN plans to leverage AB 2599 as momentum to turn the task force’s broader recommendations into law. "It helps us move the work of the task force from recommendations toward implementation," Nimmers said. "This is really an important, big victory for our alliance and for our work with reparations task force members, but it is also just one step in a much greater movement and effort that we're trying to be a part of." The California Black Power Network is a statewide coalition composed of 48 Black-led and Black-serving organizations operating across 14 California counties. Bringing together grassroots organizations focused on housing, education and criminal justice reform, CBPN was established to combat systemic racism through policy advocacy and community organizing. Central to the network’s mission is reparative justice. CBPN frames present-day economic disparities — including educational gaps, wealth inequality and systemic injustice — as direct consequences of historical harms stemming from chattel slavery, segregation, and Jim Crow practices. During the multi-year tenure of the California Task Force to Study and Develop Reparation Proposals for African Americans (established under AB 3121), CBPN served as an official state community anchor. The coalition facilitated grassroots civic engagement across California, hosting listening sessions to gather public testimony that directly informed the task force’s landmark 1,100-page final report issued in 2023. With AB 2599 now on the books, CBPN is focused on expanding its grassroots base to push for full implementation. CALIFORNIA COUNTY APPROVES REPARATIONS PLAN AS NEIGHBORING SCHOOL DISTRICT 'BLACK THRIVING' EFFORT STALLS "AB 2599 really represents a historic step toward corporate transparency and accountability," Nimmers said. "We know for generations, corporations and financial institutions have really benefited from slavery and from the exploitation of Black people. AB 2599 is starting to establish a process for qualifying corporations doing business in California to really examine and disclose any historical ties they've had to slavery. This matters because we can't fully and meaningfully repair harms if we're not really willing to acknowledge and confront the truth," she added. "When we're thinking about what repair looks like," she said, "it's important that we're tying it back to what the origin of it was so we can address those core issues." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Elsewhere in the country, localized reparations programs have moved forward with mixed success. Black residents in Evanston, Illinois, received $25,000 housing grants as part of a municipal program aimed at rectifying historic housing discrimination. Similar local and municipal initiatives seeking to provide direct compensation or economic aid are being debated nationwide.

articles.title: Cornell bans fraternity parties for the rest of the academic year amid investigation into alleged sexual assault
articles.summary: The university will also bring on “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators” to review allegations of sexual assault on campus.
articles.body: Cornell University said Tuesday it is suspending all “parties and social events” at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid an uproar over a former student’s allegation that she was sexually assaulted by members of the campus Chi Phi chapter nearly two years ago. Michael I. Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, also announced that the Ivy League institution would bring on “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators” to review allegations of sexual assault on campus. “These are first steps toward systemic change on our campus,” Kotlikoff said in a statement posted on Cornell’s website. “We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors.” The former student, identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, alleges she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit last month against multiple parties, including the university, the fraternity, her sorority, Tri Delta, and seven former Chi Phi members. Attorneys for four of the men have said their clients deny sexually assaulting Jane Doe or coercing her with drugs. The three other men have not responded to requests for comment. None of the seven has been criminally charged. The fraternity and the sorority previously declined to discuss the pending litigation. Jane Doe’s lawsuit put renewed scrutiny on the Cornell University Police Department’s handling of the 2024 probe and the local district attorney office’s decision not to bring criminal charges. Cornell and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten have defended their investigations, with the prosecutor saying his office was not provided with all the materials from the campus police investigation. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to oversee the case going forward. Cornell separately tasked former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates with an independent review of how the school responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus. “I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” Kotlikoff said in Tuesday’s announcement. “It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.” Tuesday’s announcement outlined other changes in response to the Jane Doe case, including additional staff members at the Cornell Office of Civil Rights. In response to a request for comment, Jane Doe’s lawyer said his client’s “goal in filing her lawsuit was not solely for herself.” “She wanted to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims. While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe,” said the lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. “However, these steps will hopefully go a long way to help ensure that there are no more Jane Does.”

articles.title: Anthropic says its A.I. model submitted a false cold case tip to Philadelphia police
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence research company Anthropic says one of its models generated a bogus tip about an unsolved murder and submitted it to Philadelphia police.
articles.body: Artificial intelligence research company Anthropic says one of its models generated a bogus tip about an unsolved murder and submitted it to Philadelphia police, warning that the incident raises concerns about high tech “behaviors” that “could do far more harm as models become more powerful.” The A.I. model reached out to PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18 and made a “false homicide tip,” the Philadelphia Police Department said Tuesday in a statement. The tip, though, was flagged as spam by the agency and was never forwarded to investigators, police said. The department emphasized that all tips have to go through human vetting before ever getting an a detective’s desk. “The department’s regular investigative process for crime tips requires human review and vetting before any tips are disseminated for investigative follow-up,” the department said. “Regardless of who submits information or how it reaches the department, a tip is a lead to assess — not an established fact. Investigators evaluate its credibility and seek corroborating evidence,” the statement said. “An automated submission does not bypass that process.” Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 4.5 “had been tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages,” according to a company statement. And in one run on July 18, Claude “landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide” and came to a page that “contained a tip form run by a police department,” Anthropic said. Claude filled out an online form with: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” While Anthropic insisted no harm was done, the company said it takes these kind of unintended model actions seriously. While this case “had minimal impact, we do not want to diminish the findings, because the same behaviors could do far more harm as models become more powerful,” the company said. The disclosure from Anthropic shows just one example of many recent actions taken by AI agents from various companies that weren’t predicted or intended by their human operators. Anthropic, the San Francisco-based A.I. titan, is a private company that has taken initial steps that could lead to one of the biggest initial public offerings in Wall Street history.

articles.title: A Kentucky man died without a will with about $2.33 million in transfer-on-death investment accounts left to his children; an appeals court has upheld his widow’s right to half the accounts plus part of earlier gifts
articles.summary: A Kentucky woman whose husband died without leaving a will has won a legal dispute over approximately $2.33 million held in investment accounts that named
articles.body: A Kentucky woman whose husband died without leaving a will has won a legal dispute over approximately $2.33 million held in investment accounts that named his children as beneficiaries. The Kentucky Court of Appeals has upheld an earlier ruling that Nancy Bobo Perrine is entitled to half the value of the accounts, along with a share of $126,000 in gifts made to her husband's children and grandchildren shortly before his death.The ruling, issued on Friday concerns the estate of William E. Perrine, known as Bill, who died on February 6, 2024. His four adult children challenged a Fayette Circuit Court decision that recognised Nancy's legal right to a portion of his personal property under Kentucky's dower law.According to court records, the dispute arose because Bill had named his children, rather than his wife, as beneficiaries of two investment accounts. These were transfer-on-death (TOD) accounts, which allow assets to pass directly to named beneficiaries when the account holder dies. However, the appeals court found that the arrangement did not remove Nancy's statutory claim to the money.The judges also agreed with the lower court that the children had failed to overcome a legal presumption that the arrangements were intended to deprive Nancy of her rightful share.Couple married without financial agreementBill and Nancy first met in Atlanta in 1952, when Bill was studying at the Georgia Institute of Technology. They dated briefly before Bill returned to Kentucky. The two then went their separate ways for about 50 years.Bill married, had four children and later divorced. Nancy married John Bobo in 1955 and had three children. Her husband died in 2002.Bill and Nancy reconnected in 2007 while living in different cities. They eventually married in October 2015, after which Nancy moved to Lexington. The court noted that they had neither discussed their personal finances nor signed a prenuptial or postnuptial agreement.Bill suffered a serious fall in December 2022, that required months of hospital treatment. He died in February 2024 without a will and Nancy was appointed to administer his estate.The $2.33 million investment accountsAt the time of his death, Bill owned no real estate, and his tangible personal property was valued at $18,826. However, he held an IRA and another investment account managed through Schwab, together worth $2,331,762.92.Both accounts named his children as transfer-on-death beneficiaries. The court also examined an earlier investment account held with Baird Private Wealth Management with a balance of $409,395 in May 2022.In 2023, Bill's son, under a power of attorney, designated the children as beneficiaries of the Baird account. He later closed it and moved the funds into the investment account which became part of the Schwab holdings.Bill also held two fully paid whole-life insurance policies worth a combined $2 million, with his children as beneficiaries. Nancy did not claim any portion of those proceeds because of the applicable legal treatment of life insurance.Another disputed transaction occurred on January 30, 2024, just one week before Bill died. His son arranged seven payments of $18,000 each from the Schwab investment account to Bill's children and grandchildren worth $126,000..Matter reaches courtNancy filed a civil case in Fayette Circuit Court in April 2024, seeking recognition of her dower rights and raising claims involving fraud on dower and conversion.Under the version of Kentucky law applicable when Bill died, a surviving spouse of someone who died without a will was entitled to half of the surplus personal property. In October 2025, the circuit court ruled in Nancy's favour.Bill's children appealed, arguing that the accounts passed outside probate and therefore should not be included in the property subject to Nancy's claim.They also argued that Bill had originally selected his children as beneficiaries before reconnecting with Nancy, meaning the arrangements were not intended to deny her an inheritance.The appeals court disagreed with both arguments. It explained that although transfer-on-death accounts pass directly to beneficiaries and the account holder retains ownership and control during their lifetime.It also said that Bill could withdraw money, change beneficiaries or close the accounts without obtaining his children's permission. The court therefore said that the assets remained his property until his death and were subject to Nancy's statutory interest.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Israel’s Yellow Line in Gaza advances, leaving displaced with nowhere to go
articles.summary: As Israel moves Gaza’s Yellow Line westward, displaced families in Shujayea face renewed danger.
articles.body:
Shujayea, Gaza Strip – Mahmoud Harzeen is pitching a tent about 200 metres from the yellow concrete blocks marking Israel’s so-called Yellow Line , preparing for his sixth move.

Each time the line inches closer, the 35-year-old packs up and moves further back, trying to keep his family away from danger. But every move offers only temporary relief.

“Every time they move forward a little, we move back a little,” Harzeen told Al Jazeera.

The Yellow Line divided Gaza’s territory between Israeli and Palestinian control as part of the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement.

Israeli forces withdrew behind the line, but have continued to move the demarcation deeper into Gaza. They now control about 65 percent of Gaza, according to the United Nations, up from the 53 percent agreed a year ago.

On October 11, Israeli forces moved the yellow concrete blocks dozens of metres westward in Shujayea, in eastern Gaza City. More of the neighbourhood was brought under Israeli military control and Palestinian families were forced to flee again, with Israel’s shifting boundaries further restricting where they can live and move.

For Harzeen, who supports a family of 10, the latest move is part of a year-long search for somewhere his family can live.

He can’t remember the dates of each displacement. Instead, he recalled the places, one after another: Zeitoun, Sahat al-Shawa, al-Muntazah.

“About six times – every time the line advanced a little – I would feel that it was dangerous, so I would move back a little and try to live there for a while,” he explained.

His most recent move barely lasted one night. After spending time setting up the tent, he slept in it once before Israeli forces moved the Yellow Line forward again, getting too close for Harzeen’s liking.

“I pitched the tent and slept in it for one night,” he said. “The next morning, we took our bedding and our things and left.”

The threat extends beyond the movement of the blocks themselves. Harzeen described living amid drones, helicopters, artillery fire and stray bullets, with shrapnel posing a constant danger to people sheltering nearby.

The nights when the line advances are particularly frightening, he said, recalling tanks, troops and heavy shelling as the blocks were moved.

Israel has continued its attacks despite the “ceasefire”, killing nearly 1,500 Palestinians in the last year. Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since the war started in October 2023.

“The night they move the line, there are tanks, infantry coming down, and shells being fired,” he said. “All of that happens just so they can move the yellow block a little further forward.”

Most people in Gaza have been displaced multiple times as a result of Israel’s genocidal war and the accompanying large scale destruction of buildings across the enclave. That leaves little space to pitch tents in safer areas and soaring rent that Harzeen can’t afford.

Now he is preparing for the possibility of moving again. “They will probably move it forward again,” he said. “Every time we have to flee, we have to move closer to it. We keep moving.”

Fleeing at night, returning in the morning

For Asma Ali, 32, the Yellow Line’s advance has turned displacement into a cycle of fleeing at night and returning in the morning, never knowing how long her family can stay in one place.

Ali, a mother of three from Shujayea, said her family has been displaced seven or eight times since the ceasefire began.

After staying in central Gaza City, they returned to Shujayea hoping to settle in the al-Mantar area. But then, a month later, renewed shelling and evacuation fears forced them to move again.

The family sought shelter at a school before moving to a house near a bus stop. After a night of heavy shelling, they left in the early hours of the morning and went to stay with family back in the centre of Gaza City. But the advance of the Yellow Line has left Ali uncertain about where her family could go next.

“Every night, we would flee, then come back in the morning,” Ali said. “You spend the night trying to find somewhere to stay, then return the next morning.”

“The night the Yellow Line advances is terrifying,” she said. “The shooting continues from the beginning of the night until dawn. You live in fear.”

Ali said her family lost their belongings – including gold, household items and her children’s clothes – when the dwelling they were staying in was destroyed.

Among the items lost was a brace for her son, who has a disability. She only had the brace for two days.

“It was gone in the blink of an eye,” she said.

The family has been trying to find somewhere safe to stay, but Ali said there is nowhere they can afford to go. Moving south is also difficult, with transport hard to find and little certainty that they will find a safe place there.

Asma’s request is simple: somewhere her children can sleep without the family having to flee again.

“The most important thing is somewhere safe for us,” she said. “Somewhere I can put my children and where we can rest and settle.”

articles.title: Pak police fire tear gas, live rounds at protesters in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; 50 detained
articles.summary: Pakistan police on Tuesday fired tear gas and live rounds at protesters in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as clashes broke out over the suspension of the provincial
articles.body: Pakistan police on Tuesday fired tear gas and live rounds at protesters in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as clashes broke out over the suspension of the provincial government led by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).Five people were injured in the clashes, with the worst violence reported in Bara, around 15 km from provincial capital Peshawar, Reuters reported.Police said 50 people had been detained and would face terrorism and sabotage charges for allegedly damaging government property and disrupting law and order.A police official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said protesters set fire to a National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) centre in Bara. PTI information secretary Ikram Khatana, however, said unidentified people had started the fire and also stormed nearby offices.Pakistan suspended the provincial government amid worsening law and order and an escalating confrontation between the PTI-led administration and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government.President Asif Ali Zardari issued the proclamation under Articles 232(1) and 234(1) of the Constitution, citing a surge in terrorist attacks and a breakdown of constitutional machinery in the province. The move stripped the elected provincial administration of its powers, requiring the chief minister, provincial ministers, advisers, special assistants and advocate general to vacate their offices.The presidential declaration cited the grave security situation and alleged failure of the provincial government to contain militancy as reasons for imposing the emergency.“The extraordinary intensity of terrorist incidents poses serious threats to the lives and property of the public,” the declaration said.The removal of PTI’s only provincial government marks another setback for Imran, who has been in prison since 2023.Khan faces charges including inciting riots targeting military installations and corruption. articles.title: Lawyers for Charlie Kirk's accused assassin Tyler Robinson want cameras banned after report on taxpayer burden
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson's defense lawyers argue that cameras at the upcoming hearing could threaten his right to a fair trial in the Charlie Kirk case.
articles.body: Lawyers for accused Charlie Kirk assassin Tyler Robinson are again asking a Utah judge to block cameras from the courtroom, this time ahead of a hearing where a trial date could be set — as they warn that scrutiny over the cost of his defense may be creating a risk to his right to a fair trial. The hearing is not expected to include witness testimony, but Robinson's lawyers argue that ongoing coverage of Kirk's murder could have an "incremental adverse effect" that outweighs the benefit of video coverage to the public's understanding of court proceedings. "Only a few weeks ago, the media reported on costs associated with the defense," his lawyers wrote Monday in an opposition filing from local media to send a camera to cover the Oct. 23 hearing. "Against that backdrop, statements by defense counsel at the upcoming proceeding concerning the time and resources necessary to prepare this case are likely to be examined and disseminated in real time through social media and other media channels and viewed through the lens of cost, rather than in the context of Mr. Robinson’s constitutional rights to the effective assistance of counsel, a fair trial, due process of law, and a reliable penalty determination." JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAIN WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE The Salt Lake Tribune reported that Utah County had paid $1.6 million to Robinson's legal team as of last month, exhausting a special $1 million earmark from the state. High-profile murder cases can cost millions to defend, especially if they go to trial. GOT A TIP? Overhead typically includes expert witnesses, defense investigations, lab testing and more. Some experts have predicted Robinson's defense could cost as much as $10 million. JUDGE ALLOWS CAMERAS IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION CASE, DELAYS PRELIMINARY HEARING Additional coverage, his lawyers argued, "risks reinforcing existing prejudicial perceptions of Mr. Robinson and his defense." Robinson's lawyers have repeatedly attempted to have cameras — for both still photography and video — blocked from the courtroom, arguing for various reasons that they violate his right to a fair trial. articles.title: DR Congo Ebola cases pass 9,000 as efforts to curb transmission falter
articles.summary: The Bundibugyo strain fuels deadliest Ebola outbreak in DRC’s history as health workers face mistrust from communities.
articles.body:
Confirmed Ebola cases have surpassed 9,000 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) outbreak, according to Health Ministry data, as efforts to stifle transmission falter.

The ministry reported 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths on Tuesday – a death toll of nearly half the known cases.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has become the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history. Globally, the toll is only second to the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic, which saw 28,600 confirmed cases and more than 11,000 deaths across Guinea, ⁠⁠Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The Bundibugyo strain currently has no approved vaccines or treatments and has raised concerns over cross-border transmission.

Last week, Kenya reported its first imported case in which a Kenyan national who lived in the DRC travelled through Uganda before reaching Nairobi, where he died.

Uganda also reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but the country was declared Ebola-free in August.

The current outbreak in the DRC was announced in mid-May, but some experts suspect it began as early as February. The virus, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids, has spread to seven provinces in the north and east.

Efforts to contain the virus face obstacles as health workers and other responders in the DRC face mistrust in local communities, with many believing the disease is a ruse for officials to siphon off money . The outbreak is also occurring amid an ongoing conflict between the M23 rebel group and government forces, making transport of healthcare resources to remote regions difficult.

A local politician in eastern DRC was beaten to death in September after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radio, according to his political party.

A clinical trial to evaluate vaccine efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain is being prepared for the DRC in the coming weeks, WHO Health Emergencies Programme Executive Director Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu said on Tuesday.

articles.title: Decorated San Francisco police officer and her daughter killed by her husband in suspected murder-suicide
articles.summary: The San Francisco Police Department was in mourning Tuesday after a trailblazing police officer and her husband, who also had worked for the department, were found dead along with their daughter in what investigators are calling a “suspected double-murder suicide.”
articles.body: The San Francisco Police Department was in mourning Tuesday after a trailblazing police officer and her husband, who also had worked for the department, were found dead along with their daughter in what investigators are calling a “suspected double-murder suicide.” Retired Sgt. Kevin Mannix, 68, fatally shot his wife, Ann Mannix, 64, a retired deputy chief, and their 24-year-old daughter, Katherine Elizabeth Mannix, around 5 p.m. Sunday before turning the gun on himself, the Marin County Sheriff’s Office said. Police found their bodies after responding to a home in a neighborhood just north of the city following a 911 call from a person “who safely exited the residence.” Investigators have not released a motive for the mayhem and autopsies were scheduled Tuesday for all three individuals. Meanwhile, the San Francisco PD was trying to absorb the loss. “The tragic loss of retired Deputy Chief Ann Mannix, her daughter Katie, and retired Sergeant Kevin Mannix in a suspected murder-suicide has left our entire SFPD family reeling,” the San Francisco Police Officers Association said in a statement posted online. “There are no words that can fully capture the depth of this tragedy, nor are there simple answers to the painful questions we are all asking.” Kevin Mannix worked for the SFPD for 27 years before retiring from the department in 2018 with the rank of sergeant, according to the department. But it was his wife who left the biggest mark on the department. A fourth-generation San Franciscan with several relatives who had previously worked as police officers, Ann Mannix joined the SFPD in 1986 a little over a decade after it started to hire women as patrol officers, The San Francisco Chronicle reported. Ann Mannix rose steadily through the ranks, from lieutenant in 2003 to commander in 2015 and to deputy chief in 2018. Before retiring in 2021, she led the field operations and special operations bureaus, the police department said in a statement. And she was the first woman to be part of and later lead the SWAT team.

articles.title: New rule for H-1B again? Visa extensions will be treated as fresh cases; asylum seekers and H-4 visa holders will also be affected
articles.summary: Again a new rule dropped from the Department of Homeland Security that will concern H-1B visa holders.
articles.body: Again a new rule dropped from the Department of Homeland Security that will concern H-1B visa holders. But the scope of the new rule will be far greater than just H-1Bs. It will impact anyone with a work authorization in the US as the DHS issued a rule eliminating a grace period for immigrants whose work authorization expires while renewal applications are still pending.The measure released Tuesday makes permanent an interim final rule DHS issued last year doing away with a 540-day automatic extension period adopted under the Biden administration. The agency said the change, which affects asylum seekers as well as spouses of H-1B specialty occupation workers, would allow for more frequent vetting of applicants, Bloomberg reported.The extension window was designed to ensure immigrant workers aren’t pushed out of jobs because of processing delays at US Citizenship and Immigration Services.The final rule will take effect after it’s published in the Federal Register on October 14 with a 30-day public comment period.As of June 30, more than 432,000 work permit renewal applications were pending at USCIS for six months, including more than 91,000 for more than a year and a half. Foreign workers aren’t eligible to re-up the documents until 180 days before their expiration date, the Bloomberg report said. A group of H-4 visa holders sued DHS in January, arguing the policy change violated the Administrative Procedure Act. A California judge last month enjoined the interim final rule for those plaintiffs, finding it didn’t follow procedural requirements or acknowledge the reliance interests of plaintiffs, the report added.What is the new rule?Extensions of work authorizations of H-1Bs and H-4s now do not attract the same scrutiny as these people have already been working and if they are applying for an extension with the same employers and the same job, the USCIS does not treat it as a fresh case but now it will.This means there will be more denials, more documentation, more RFEs.
